purpose: Inotuzumab ozogamicin is used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in adults. It is specifically used when the cancer has come back or has not responded to other treatments. Your doctor may recommend this medicine when other options have not worked well enough.
how_it_works: Think of this medicine as a guided missile. It has two parts: one part is a special protein (antibody) that seeks out and locks onto cancer cells by recognizing a specific target called CD22 found on the surface of leukemia cells. Once it attaches, it delivers a powerful cell-killing drug directly into the cancer cell, destroying it from the inside while trying to leave healthy cells alone.
common_side_effects: Low blood counts (which can cause tiredness, easy bruising, or increased risk of infection), nausea, headache, fever, low blood pressure, increased liver enzyme levels, belly pain, and fatigue. Most side effects are manageable with supportive care.
warnings: This medicine carries serious risks including liver problems, especially a serious condition called veno-occlusive disease (VOD) where blood flow in the liver is blocked — this can be life-threatening. It also increases your risk of serious infections due to low blood cell counts. It should not be used during pregnancy as it can harm an unborn baby. Regular blood tests and liver checks are very important during treatment. Tell your doctor immediately if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, sudden weight gain, or severe belly pain.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an IV (intravenous) infusion directly into your vein in a hospital or clinic setting. It is usually given in treatment cycles — commonly on days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle. Your doctor will determine the exact dose based on your body size and overall health. You will be monitored closely during and after each infusion.
